newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.

text.p: HOWARD APPLAUDS TOYOTA EXPANSION
Toyota's decision to build a new luxury car in Australia vindicates the Federal Government's retention of tariff levels in the automotive industry, according to Prime Minister John Howard.
The car, to be based on the US Avalon model, will be built at Toyota's Altona plant in Victoria.
Toyota has said 20,000 cars will be built each year, with the first due to roll off the production line early in 2000.
Mr Howard told Toyota officials in Melbourne this morning that freezing tariffs at 15 per cent from 2000 to 2004 was a wise choice.
"We took a decision in June to maintain our commitment to the APEC goal of free trade by the year 2010," he said.
"But we also recognised that, in the interim, a greater degree of predictability and certainty and stability were needed."
The national secretary of the vehicle builders' division of the Australian Metal Workers Union, Ian Jones, said the expansion was good news for jobs in the industry.
"It will clearly have spin-offs in terms of the components manufacturing sector and that's going to create jobs," he said.
ANGER OVER CABINET BID TO QUASH HEROIN TRIAL
A likely Federal Cabinet decision to reject a proposed heroin trial in the Australian Capital Territory has angered the ACT Chief Minister, Kate Carnell.
Cabinet Ministers have said the proposal was unlikely to survive past tomorrow's Cabinet meeting, despite a go-ahead from a majority of Australian health ministers.
Last week, Prime Minister John Howard said he was profoundly sceptical of the proposed trial, remaining unconvinced of any social benefit.
Mrs Carnell said she was angry the Federal Government had responded to a Sydney-based scare campaign, calling on Cabinet to show some leadership on a difficult issue.
"I suppose I'll never give up hope that we will see leadership in this country with regard to drug law reform and with regard to drug treatment for people with heroin addiction," she said.
"But I have to say if the Federal Government knock it off, the trial's dead in the water.
"We can't go anywhere without Federal Government support."
ARCO PLANS TO SELL AUSTRALIAN ASSETS - EXCEPT CURRAGH
American mining company ARCO expects to put its worldwide coal assets on the market this month.
The only exception will be the company's Curragh coal mine in Central Queensland, which is at the centre of a prolonged industrial dispute.
Company chief executive Bill Wegener said ARCO did not want to sell Curragh until it was operating successfully.
Mr Wegener said the remaining Australian assets that would be put on the market included the Gordonstone and Blair Athol mines and the coal reserves at Clermont, all in Central Queensland.
Meanwhile, the miners' union said pickets would continue at Curragh today when management was expected to make another attempt to move coal out by train.
Union representative Ray Coleman said workers were planning a peaceful protest.
"We don't believe the train will go through," he said.
"Probably that's all I can say at this stage."
EARLY ACTION URGED AGAINST PREDICTED MEASLES OUTBREAK
Federal Health Minister Michael Wooldridge has predicted a measles epidemic for next year and has urged non English-speaking parents to immunise their children to help contain the outbreak.
Dr Wooldridge said preventable diseases such as measles and whooping cough could be conquered if parents were given the correct information.

He said most non English-speaking parents did not have cultural reasons not to immunise their children, and he has promoted a new community education program aimed at breaking down the language barriers to immunisation.
"We can plan or predict when measles is going to hit and we are expecting a big outbreak next year," Dr Wooldridge said.
"One in every 20,000 children who get measles we could expect to die. That's why we are going to have a measles catch-up campaign next year.
"We're planning for it already, but it's very serious."
UNIVERSITIES FIGHT BACK OVER BAD PUBLICITY IN ASIA
Australia's eight richest universities have launched a joint campaign to counter negative publicity in Asia, which they claim is jeopardising millions of dollars of income from overseas students.
The Group of Eight said the bad publicity created by Independent MP Pauline Hanson was affecting the lucrative South-East Asian market, which was now a major source of income for universities.

The universities' vice-chancellors said the reputation of older institutions had also been damaged by The Good Universities Guide, which rated them lower on student satisfaction than newer universities.
Sydney University vice-chancellor Professor Gavin Brown said they had been forced to defend their position.

"We intend to set up our own network in South-East Asia of information offices, so that we can get on with the business of making sure there is excellent Australian higher education being demonstrated to people," he said.
EALES TEST DECISION DELAYED
A decision on whether Australian captain John Eales will play in Saturday's rugby union Test against South Africa is unlikely to be made until the side arrives in Pretoria.
The champion second rower will train in Sydney today with the Wallaby squad after missing Saturday's Test loss to New Zealand in Dunedin.
Selectors will meet at the same time to decide on the squad's composition for the match to be played at Pretoria.
Australia leaves for Durban tomorrow and will travel to Pretoria on Friday.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
